authoritySource: Dr. Ahmed Hesham — The Tutor Book — OET Writing Comprehensive Rulebook (Sessions 1–10) — adapted for Podiatry (Phase D v1)

rules.title: Six OET letter types
rules.body: Six OET letter types: Routine Referral, Urgent Referral, Discharge Letter, Transfer Letter, Referral to Non-Medical Professional, and Referral to GP.

rules.title: Default is Routine Referral
rules.body: Any referral task without the word 'urgent' = Routine Referral by default.

rules.title: Assessment / management requests are routine
rules.body: Case notes requesting 'assessment' or 'management from a specialist' without 'urgent' = Routine Referral.

rules.title: Urgent identifiers
rules.body: Urgent identifiers: 'urgent referral/assessment', 'admit to hospital', 'hospital admission', 'request acute management', 'as soon as possible (ASAP)', 'acutely unwell', 'for immediate assessment'.

rules.title: Suspected cancer: preserve urgency as supported
rules.body: Suspected cancer does not automatically define task type independently of the task/context; preserve urgency exactly as supported.

rules.title: Discharge letter identifiers
rules.body: Discharge letter identifiers: 'write a discharge letter', patient described as in hospital or being discharged, you are writing from hospital to GP.

rules.title: Non-medical professional list
rules.body: Non-medical professionals: OT, physiotherapist, social worker, psychologist, dietitian, speech pathologist, pharmacist, care facility manager. Nurse is classified as medical, not non-medical.

rules.title: Cancer screening vs suspected cancer
rules.body: Do not confuse routine cancer screening referrals with urgent referrals for suspected cancer.

rules.title: Total exam time 45 minutes
rules.body: Total exam time: 45 minutes.

rules.title: Five-minute reading-only window
rules.body: First 5 minutes = reading time only. No writing is permitted; pen must remain down.

rules.title: Target 30 minutes writing + 10 minutes review
rules.body: Remaining 40 minutes = writing time. Practice target: finish in 30 minutes, leaving 10 minutes for review.

rules.title: Paper layout
rules.body: Paper 1 = case notes (usually 2 pages). Paper 2 / Booklet = writing answer sheet.

rules.title: Written task elements
rules.body: The written task (bottom of case notes) states: letter type, recipient name + address, request, and sometimes the diagnosis.

rules.title: Diagnosis location fallback
rules.body: If diagnosis is absent from the written task, check the 'plan' section immediately above it.

rules.title: Today's date = letter date
rules.body: 'Today's date' at the top of case notes = the date of the letter.

rules.title: Diagnosis types treated identically
rules.body: Diagnosis types — provisional, preliminary, evaluatory, confirmatory — are treated identically in OET letters.

rules.title: Three data categories
rules.body: All data falls into one of three categories: Relevant (must include), Irrelevant (must exclude), Semi-relevant (include if letter is short; exclude if long).

rules.title: Marks for inclusion AND exclusion
rules.body: Marks are awarded for INCLUDING relevant data AND for EXCLUDING irrelevant data. Content selection is the single most important OET writing skill.

rules.title: Recipient specialty drives relevance
rules.body: The recipient specialty determines relevance. Ask: 'Would this specialist need this to manage the patient?'

rules.title: Smoking and drinking included when relevant
rules.body: Smoking/alcohol are not universal always-include facts; relevance and reader needs control content.

rules.title: Divorce / living situation — conditional
rules.body: Divorce, living situation, number of children: include only if directly relevant to the specialty.

rules.title: Allergy inclusion is relevance/safety driven
rules.body: Allergy inclusion is relevance/safety driven; the atopic-condition rule is a heuristic, not an official absolute.

rules.title: Family history — conditional
rules.body: Family history: include only if a family member has a related condition.

rules.title: Letter length guide 180–200 words
rules.body: Letter length guide: 180–200 words (body only). Too long = semi-relevant data included. Too short = relevant data missing.

rules.title: Max 4 body paragraphs
rules.body: Maximum 4 body paragraphs. Typical: 2–3 body paragraphs. Paper-based: fills to approx two-thirds of second page.

rules.title: Letter structure order
rules.body: Letter structure order: Address → [blank] → Date → [blank] → Salutation → Re: line → Introduction → [blank] → Body paragraphs (each separated by blank line) → [blank] → Closure → [blank] → Yours sincerely/faithfully → [1–2 blank lines] → professional designation only, e.g. Doctor (owner Rev8, OWN-W-026).

rules.title: No blank line between Salutation and Re: line
rules.body: NO blank line between the Salutation and the Re: line. They are on consecutive lines. Salutation and Re: line are the ONLY two consecutive lines with no blank line between them.

rules.title: Computer-based Enter convention
rules.body: Computer-based exam: two Enter presses = one blank line. 'Space' or 'blank line' throughout this rulebook means 1–2 Enters on the keyboard.

rules.title: One blank line between body paragraphs
rules.body: Each body paragraph is separated from the next by exactly one blank line.

rules.title: Address components
rules.body: Address components: recipient name, specialty, clinic name, street, city/town. Number of lines varies; not always five.

rules.title: Address capitalisation and punctuation
rules.body: Address: first letter of each component = CAPITAL. No commas or full stops. Use Enter (not comma) between components.

rules.title: Address copied from case notes
rules.body: Address is always copied directly from the written task in the case notes.

rules.title: Date = today's visit date
rules.body: Date of the letter = date of today's visit (at top of case notes).

rules.title: Date format consistency
rules.body: Date format must be consistent throughout the letter. Acceptable formats: DD/MM/YYYY, 1 January 2024, 01/01/2024, 1st January 2024.

rules.title: Never abbreviate the year
rules.body: Never abbreviate the year (write 2024, not '24).

rules.title: Leading zero for single-digit dates
rules.body: Numbers 1–9 in dates: always add a leading zero (01, 02 … 09).

rules.title: No 'Date:' prefix
rules.body: Do NOT write the word 'Date:' before the date.

rules.title: One blank line above and below date
rules.body: The date has exactly ONE blank line above it and ONE blank line below it.

rules.title: Standard salutation form
rules.body: Standard: Dear Dr. [Last Name], — capital D, lowercase r. Always use LAST name, never first name.

rules.title: Optional comma / dot
rules.body: Comma after salutation: optional. Dot after Dr/Mr/Ms: optional.

rules.title: No blank line between salutation and Re:
rules.body: No blank line between salutation and Re: line.

rules.title: Special salutations
rules.body: Special salutations: No name given → Dear Doctor. Nurse/OT/Radiographer without name → Dear Sir/Madam. Admissions Officer → Dear Admissions Officer. Emergency Registrar → Dear Emergency Registrar. Assistant Professor → Dear Assistant Professor. UK surgeon → 'Mr [Last Name]' acceptable.

rules.title: Non-medical salutation rules
rules.body: Non-medical professional — no name: Dear Sir/Madam. Name given: Dear Mr/Ms [Last Name].

rules.title: Re: line format
rules.body: Re: line format: Re: [Title] [Full Name] D.O.B: [date]. Both 'Re:' and 'RE:' are acceptable.

rules.title: Re: line full name; body last name only
rules.body: Re: line = full name (first + last). In body: LAST NAME + TITLE only (e.g., Ms Miller); children: first name only. Never repeat the full name after the Re: line, the introduction included (owner Rev8, OWN-W-011).

rules.title: Age / DOB handling in Re: line
rules.body: When only DOB is given → write DOB in Re: line. When only age is given → write 'aged [X]' (lowercase, no colon) after the full name. Do NOT write the age again in the introduction. When both are given → use DOB in Re: line; age is optional in the introduction.

rules.title: Age forms in running text
rules.body: Age in running text (three acceptable forms): 'Age: 25' / '25 years old' / '25 years of age'.

rules.title: Children: no title; first name in body
rules.body: Children (Day 1 of life up to and including 17 years old): NO title in Re: line — write full name only. In the body: use FIRST NAME only. At 18 years old the patient becomes an adult and receives a title (Mr/Ms/Miss). Never write 'Master' for boys.

rules.title: Yours sincerely vs faithfully
rules.body: 'Yours sincerely' when recipient name is known. 'Yours faithfully' when no name (Dear Sir/Madam, Dear Doctor).

rules.title: Yours sincerely capitalisation
rules.body: Capitalisation: Yours (capital Y), sincerely (lowercase s). Spelling: S-I-N-C-E-R-E-L-Y.

rules.title: Signature: professional designation only
rules.body: Write the professional designation only (the writer's profession, e.g. Doctor, Dietitian, Optometrist) below the closing phrase, unless the task supplies the exact writer name; never add a hospital, department, address, phone or email beneath it. Allow 1-2 blank lines between the closing phrase and the designation (owner Rev8, OWN-W-026).

rules.title: Introduction concise
rules.body: Introduction must be concise: 2–3 sentences maximum, fewest words possible.

rules.title: Intro must contain identity + purpose
rules.body: Introduction must contain: (a) Unique Identity of the patient, and (b) Purpose / Request.

rules.title: Purpose/Request mandatory
rules.body: Purpose/Request = MOST IMPORTANT element. Never omit it.

rules.title: Unique identity elements
rules.body: Unique identity elements: name, age (if not in header), occupation, summary of main condition.

rules.title: Routine referral intro template
rules.body: Routine referral template: 'I am writing to refer [Title Last Name], a [age]-year-old [occupation], for [specialist] assessment and management of [condition].'
exemplarPhrases: I am writing to refer {title} {lastName}, a {age}-year-old {occupation}, for {specialist} assessment and management of {condition}.

rules.title: Urgent intro must contain 'urgent'
rules.body: Urgent referral: MUST contain the word 'urgent' — 'I am writing to urgently refer...' / 'I am writing to request urgent assessment of...'

rules.title: Discharge: no patient identity in intro
rules.body: Discharge letter to GP: Do NOT describe patient identity in introduction — GP knows the patient.

rules.title: Discharge intro template
rules.body: Discharge introduction template: 'I am writing to update you regarding Mr Jones, who underwent [procedure] at [hospital] and is now ready for discharge, for whom I am requesting your ongoing care.'
exemplarPhrases: I am writing to update you regarding {title} {lastName}, who underwent {procedure} at {hospital} and is now ready for discharge, for whom I am requesting your ongoing care.

rules.title: Avoid gentleman/lady appositives
rules.body: Gentleman/lady is unnecessary and may be dated; use patient/person or an appropriate identifier.

rules.title: Minimum 2 body paragraphs
rules.body: Minimum 2 body paragraphs. NEVER write the entire letter in one paragraph.

rules.title: Today's visit has its own paragraph
rules.body: Today's visit must always have its own paragraph. In an urgent referral it is body paragraph 1 and stays its own paragraph even when today's visit contains very little information (owner Rev8, OWN-W-017). Other letter types only: a single item of information today may be combined with the adjacent visit.

rules.title: Previous visits combined or summarised
rules.body: Previous visits may be combined or summarised. Do NOT give every visit its own paragraph.

rules.title: Subjective + Objective + Management
rules.body: Visit structure: Subjective (symptoms) + Objective (examination) + Management.

rules.title: Urgent referral: body starts with today's visit
rules.body: Urgent referral: ALWAYS begin body with TODAY'S VISIT (most acute presentation), then background chronologically.

rules.title: Prefer elapsed time over exact dates
rules.body: Visit referencing: prefer elapsed time over exact dates — '3 months ago' preferred over the exact date.

rules.title: 'Next visit' is acceptable English
rules.body: Next visit is standard English; following visit may be stylistically preferable in some narratives but is not mandatory.

rules.title: Never write today's date in body
rules.body: NEVER write today's date in the body. Use 'On today's visit' or 'On today's presentation' instead.

rules.title: No 'Yesterday'
rules.body: 'Yesterday' never used in a medical letter. Write 'one day prior' or 'one day ago' instead.

rules.title: 'Over the last X' starts a paragraph
rules.body: 'Over the last [X time]': summarises multiple visits with the same complaint. Requires present perfect. Use only to START a paragraph.

rules.title: Duration adjective hyphenation
rules.body: Duration as adjective (before noun): hyphenate, no plural: 'a 6-month history of acne'. Duration standalone: plural: 'For 6 months, she has had acne.'

rules.title: Condition change vocabulary
rules.body: Condition unchanged: 'persisted' / 'remained unchanged'. Improved: 'there was partial improvement'. Worsened: 'deteriorated' / 'worsened'.

rules.title: Advice vocabulary
rules.body: Advice: 'She was advised to adopt lifestyle changes.' / 'She was counselled regarding...' (never 'instructed to adopt').

rules.title: Never 'the patient' as the person reference
rules.body: Never use 'the patient' (or 'a patient at this practice') as a substitute for the person in the letter; use the name form (adults: title + last name, e.g. Ms Miller; children: first name) or a pronoun. Never repeat the full name after the Re: line (owner Rev8, OWN-W-009, OWN-W-011).

rules.title: Name vs pronoun pattern
rules.body: Name vs. Pronoun within paragraphs: Use the patient's name (title + last name for adults; first name for children) at the FIRST mention in each paragraph. For ALL subsequent mentions within the SAME paragraph, use a pronoun. At the start of EVERY new paragraph, use the name again.

rules.title: Closure ends with a contact offer
rules.body: Every Model Answer closure, in every letter type, ends with a professional offer of further contact, e.g. 'Should there be any queries, kindly do not hesitate to contact me.' or 'Please do not hesitate to contact me should you require further information.'; 'I trust this information will be of use.' may precede it (owner Rev8, OWN-W-014). Candidates: the same meaning anywhere in the closure, in any professional wording.
exemplarPhrases: I trust this information will be of use.
Please do not hesitate to contact me should you require further information.

rules.title: Urgent closure: 'at your earliest convenience'
rules.body: Urgent closure MUST include 'at your earliest convenience.' Spelling: C-O-N-V-E-N-I-E-N-C-E.

rules.title: Use 'urgent' once
rules.body: Use 'urgent' once in introduction only; use 'at your earliest convenience' in closure to imply urgency — do not repeat 'urgent' throughout.

rules.title: Follow-up / review date must appear
rules.body: Follow-up / review date stated in case notes → ALWAYS mention in closure.

rules.title: Enclosed results instead of dumping values
rules.body: Copy of results/imaging stated as enclosed → write 'Please find enclosed a copy of Mr [Name]'s pathology/imaging results.' Do NOT also list the values in the letter.

rules.title: Medication list attachment
rules.body: Copy of medication list attached → list medication names only (no doses).

rules.title: Patient-initiated referral
rules.body: Patient-initiated referral → 'upon his/her request' or 'at Mr Jones' request' in introduction or closure.

rules.title: Consent statement
rules.body: Consent in case notes → 'Please note that Mr Jones has been fully informed of his diagnosis and management.'

rules.title: Blank line before closing phrase
rules.body: Always leave ONE blank line before 'Yours sincerely,' / 'Yours faithfully,'. The last body paragraph and the closing phrase must be separated by a blank line.

rules.title: Intro tense options
rules.body: Introduction: present simple or present perfect (both acceptable).

rules.title: Visits = past simple
rules.body: All visits (today and previous): PAST SIMPLE. Safest choice; never wrong for visit content.

rules.title: Present perfect only if symptom persists
rules.body: Present perfect for a visit: acceptable only if the symptom is still present at time of writing. CANNOT use present perfect for vital signs.

rules.title: Ongoing facts = present simple
rules.body: Medical/social/family history — ongoing facts: present simple. 'She has hypertension.'

rules.title: 'Since' + starting point = present perfect
rules.body: 'Since' + starting point → present perfect: 'She has had hypertension since 2010.'

rules.title: 'For' + duration = present perfect
rules.body: 'For' + duration → present perfect: 'She has had hypertension for 5 years.'

rules.title: Smoking/drinking tense
rules.body: Smoking/drinking with duration → present perfect continuous: 'She has been smoking for 20 years.' Without duration → present simple: 'She smokes.'

rules.title: Procedures: past simple or present perfect by time reference
rules.body: Present perfect is valid with procedures when current relevance/no finished time supports it (has undergone).

rules.title: 'Over the last X' first sentence = present perfect
rules.body: 'Over the last [X]': first sentence → present perfect; remaining sentences in same paragraph → past simple acceptable.

rules.title: 'X ago' = past simple
rules.body: '[X] ago' → always past simple. 'She has presented 3 weeks ago' = WRONG. 'She presented 3 weeks ago' = CORRECT.

rules.title: Medical records present simple
rules.body: Medical records: 'Mr Jones' medical records reveal/show that he has [condition].' Use present simple for reveal/show.

rules.title: Past perfect is valid for earlier-past chronology
rules.body: Past perfect is valid when needed to establish earlier-past chronology; do not ban it.

rules.title: Reported speech: that-clause, ING or noun
rules.body: That-clauses are grammatically valid after report/state/mention; gerund/noun forms are alternatives, not the only forms.

rules.title: 'Next visit' → 'on the following visit'
rules.body: 'Next visit' in past narrative → 'on the following visit.' Never use 'next.'

rules.title: Translate Latin abbreviations
rules.body: Latin abbreviations MUST be translated: od/om → once a day; bd/bid → twice a day; tds/tid → three times a day; qds/qid → four times a day; stat → immediately; prn → as needed.

rules.title: Single medication format
rules.body: Single medication: Drug, dose. Example: 'Panadol, 500 mg.'

rules.title: Multiple medications format
rules.body: Multiple medications: Drug, dose; Drug, dose; and Drug, dose. (comma: drug-dose; semicolon: between pairs; 'and' before last drug.)

rules.title: Trade vs generic capitalisation
rules.body: Trade name: Capitalise (Panadol, Augmentin). Generic: lowercase (paracetamol, amoxicillin). Use one type consistently.

rules.title: Routes conventions
rules.body: Routes: 'oral' in full (never 'PO'); IM, IV, SC, SL abbreviations acceptable. Route before drug: 'oral Panadol, 500 mg.'

rules.title: Elevated / reduced phrasing
rules.body: Elevated values: 'an elevation in glucose' / 'an increased glucose level' / 'elevated glucose.' Reduced: 'a reduction in glucose' / 'a decreased glucose level.' Do not write 'a glucose' alone.

rules.title: Level article rules
rules.body: 'Glucose level' can take article: 'an increased glucose level.' Plural modifier: no article: 'increased white cell counts.'

rules.title: Relevant numerical values keep their units
rules.body: Do not always include every numerical value; include values that are relevant to purpose/reader and preserve units accurately.

rules.title: 'an MRI' / 'an X-ray'
rules.body: 'an MRI' and 'an X-ray' — both take 'an' (initial vowel sound from letter name).

rules.title: Numerals with units
rules.body: Numerals with units always: '38.5°C', '180/110 mmHg', '500 mg.'

rules.title: Clinic scheduling fractions
rules.body: Legacy fraction conversions are unsafe/incorrect as a universal rule; interpret source notation from context and never guess.

rules.title: No contractions
rules.body: NO contractions: 'do not' not 'don't'; 'I am' not 'I'm'; 'cannot' not 'can't'.

rules.title: Never 'the patient' in body
rules.body: Never use 'the patient' as the person reference in the letter; use the name form or a pronoun (owner Rev8, OWN-W-009, which supersedes the earlier 'patient is not forbidden' wording).

rules.title: No 'smoker/drinker' labels
rules.body: Never use 'smoker/drinker' as labels. Write 'she smokes' / 'she drinks alcohol.'

rules.title: Replace colloquial terms
rules.body: Use supported clinical wording rather than weak, colloquial or redundant phrasing: fatigue not tired/sluggish; MRI not MRI imaging; felt a popping sensation not felt something pop; does not currently have a GP not with no GP. Mandatory in Model Answers; advisory for candidates (owner Rev8, OWN-W-033).

rules.title: Conditions lowercase
rules.body: Medical conditions: LOWERCASE. bronchial asthma, myocardial infarction, hypertension, gastroenteritis. Capitalising these is an error.

rules.title: Eponymous diseases capitalised
rules.body: Named (eponymous) diseases: CAPITALS. Parkinson's, Crohn's, Alzheimer's, Graves', Doppler.

rules.title: Trade names and abbreviations
rules.body: Trade medication names: capitalise. Bacteria: first word capital, second lowercase (Staphylococcus aureus). Abbreviations: all capitals (MRI, CT, ECG, A&E).

rules.title: Descriptive numbers as words
rules.body: Write descriptive/general numbers as words ('every six hours for four days', 'two weeks ago', 'three children'). Use digits only for age, dates, vital signs, investigation/lab values, medication doses and clinical measurements ('500 mg'). Owner Rev8 override OWN-W-006; replaces the old 1-9 words / 10+ numerals rule.

rules.title: 'However' punctuation
rules.body: Sentence start: 'However,' (capital + comma). Joining two complete independent clauses: '...; however, ...' (semicolon before, lowercase, comma after). Do not apply the pattern mechanically when the grammar does not contain two complete clauses; adverbial use is not flagged for candidates (owner Rev8, OWN-W-022).

rules.title: 'Therefore' / 'Thus' punctuation
rules.body: Sentence start: 'Therefore,' / 'Thus,' (capital + comma). Joining two complete independent clauses: '...; therefore, ...' (semicolon before, lowercase, comma after). Adverbial use inside a clause (e.g. 'was therefore referred') is not flagged for candidates (owner Rev8, OWN-W-022).

rules.title: 'In addition' punctuation
rules.body: Sentence start: 'In addition,' / 'Additionally,' (capital + comma). Joining two complete independent clauses: '...; in addition, ...'. 'In addition to' + noun/ING takes no punctuation (R12.12) (owner Rev8, OWN-W-022).

rules.title: 'In addition to' takes noun/ING
rules.body: 'In addition to' / 'together with' / 'along with' / 'as well as': NO preceding punctuation; followed by noun or ING.

rules.title: Proximity rule
rules.body: Proximity rule (negative sentence with 'or'): verb agrees with CLOSEST subject.

rules.title: Reverse rule
rules.body: Reverse rule ('along with' / 'together with' / 'in addition to'): verb agrees with word BEFORE the linker.

rules.title: Despite vs although
rules.body: 'Despite' + noun/ING (not a full clause). 'Although' + full clause. Both acceptable.

rules.title: 'As' (because) comma
rules.body: A comma before causal as is context-dependent, not universal.

rules.title: 'For which' comma
rules.body: Comma before for which depends on whether the relative clause is non-restrictive; not every occurrence needs one.

rules.title: Coordinating adjectives
rules.body: Coordinating adjectives (same noun): comma between them.

rules.title: Sentence length 15–25 words
rules.body: Sentence length: 15–25 words target. Do not chain 3+ clauses. No comma splices.

rules.title: Max 1–2 linkers per paragraph
rules.body: Max 1–2 linkers per paragraph. Excessive linkers reduce Conciseness and Clarity score.

rules.title: Appositive commas
rules.body: Gentleman/lady is not required; use neutral professional identifiers.

rules.title: No patient labels
rules.body: Never label patients: 'anxious', 'non-compliant.' Write: 'she expressed concern about...' / 'he reported difficulty adhering to...'

rules.title: Three elements change for urgent
rules.body: Three elements change in an urgent referral: (1) Introduction contains 'urgent', (2) Closure contains 'at your earliest convenience', (3) Body starts with today's visit.

rules.title: Urgent intro must contain 'urgent'
rules.body: Introduction MUST contain 'urgent'.

rules.title: Urgent closure phrase
rules.body: Closure MUST include 'at your earliest convenience.' Do not repeat 'urgent' after the introduction.

rules.title: Urgent body starts today
rules.body: Body: ALWAYS start with TODAY'S VISIT (acute presentation), then background chronologically.

rules.title: Urgent structure
rules.body: Structure: P1 = today's emergency. P2+ = background history. Final paragraph = active medical conditions + current medications.

rules.title: Ongoing conditions on active meds must be mentioned
rules.body: Hospital urgent referral: mention every ongoing medical condition for which the person takes active medication, with the relevant current medication and dose, using only facts from the case notes (owner Rev8, OWN-W-019). Fully resolved conditions with no current medication stay excluded (R13.7).

rules.title: Exclude resolved conditions
rules.body: Fully resolved conditions with no current medications: do NOT include.

rules.title: Penicillin allergy conditional
rules.body: Penicillin allergy: include only if patient is receiving or needs antibiotics.

rules.title: Omit empty PMH paragraph
rules.body: No past medical history? Simply omit that paragraph.

rules.title: 'ASAP' → 'at your earliest convenience'
rules.body: 'ASAP' in case notes → write 'at your earliest convenience' in the letter. Never write 'ASAP.'

rules.title: A&E and ED capitalised
rules.body: A&E and ED: always capitalised (A&E, ED, Emergency Department).

rules.title: Hospital doctor → GP
rules.body: Written by hospital doctor to GP; updates GP on admission and discharge.

rules.title: Discharge intro template
rules.body: Introduction: 'I am writing to update you regarding Mr Jones, who underwent [procedure] at [hospital] and is now ready for discharge, for whom I am requesting your ongoing care.' NEVER use routine referral language.

rules.title: Discharge: no identity in intro
rules.body: Do NOT describe patient identity in introduction — GP knows the patient.

rules.title: Discharge: known history only if changed or relevant
rules.body: Social/family/past history can be relevant to discharge if it changed or affects ongoing care; do not exclude categorically.

rules.title: Discharge allergy exception
rules.body: Mention allergy only if it directly influenced treatment.

rules.title: Admission phrasing
rules.body: Admission: 'Mr Jones was admitted to [hospital] with [symptoms/condition].' Past simple. NEVER 'was presented' (incorrect passive).

rules.title: Discharge plan is most important
rules.body: Discharge plan paragraph = most important. Must include: discharge medications with doses + post-discharge instructions.

rules.title: Discharge meds format
rules.body: Discharge medications use the R11.2-R11.3 format (owner Rev8, OWN-W-023): 'Drug, dose' for one item, 'Drug, dose and Drug, dose' for two, and 'Drug, dose; Drug, dose; and Drug, dose' for three or more.

rules.title: Select the admission investigations the reader needs
rules.body: Do not list all investigations including all normal results; select what the reader needs.

rules.title: Follow-up dates mandatory in discharge
rules.body: Follow-up / review dates: ALWAYS include if stated in case notes.

rules.title: Discharge consent
rules.body: Consent: 'Please note that Mr Jones has been fully informed of his diagnosis and management.'

rules.title: Treatment FOR, not FROM
rules.body: 'Treatment FOR' not 'Treatment FROM.' Always: treated for, admitted for, referred for, managed for.

rules.title: Discharge tense follows time reference
rules.body: Discharge letters use tense according to time: past for admission events, present for current status, future/modal for plan.

rules.title: Enclose results reference
rules.body: Copy of results stated as enclosed → 'Please find enclosed a copy of Mr [Name]'s pathology results.' Do not list values.

rules.title: Non-medical list
rules.body: Non-medical professionals: OT, physiotherapist, social worker, psychologist, dietitian, speech pathologist, pharmacist, care facility manager. Nurse is medical.

rules.title: Match technicality to the recipient
rules.body: Technicality should match the recipient. Allied-health professionals may understand clinical terminology; explain/simplify for the actual reader.

rules.title: Non-medical salutation
rules.body: Salutation: Dear Sir/Madam (no name). Dear Mr/Ms [Last Name] (name given).

rules.title: Non-medical content
rules.body: Include: condition in plain language, functional impact, specific professional request, relevant social context.

rules.title: Exclude out-of-scope details
rules.body: Exclude: medical details irrelevant to the professional's scope.

rules.title: Family dentist = specialist-style
rules.body: Family dentist: does NOT know the patient — treat like a specialist; include relevant background.

rules.title: Imperative plan items = for GP
rules.body: Imperative items in the plan = for GP. Items on the referral request line = for the specialist. Never ask the specialist to perform GP tasks.

rules.title: Mental health referral conventions
rules.body: Mental health referrals: correlate symptoms across visits; include review date; include consent statement if mentioned; include 'upon his/her request' if patient initiated.

rules.title: Six marking criteria
rules.body: Six marking criteria: (1) Purpose — max 3 marks; (2) Content — max 7; (3) Conciseness & Clarity — max 7; (4) Genre & Style — max 7; (5) Organisation & Layout — max 7; (6) Language — max 7.

rules.title: Purpose 0–3 scale only
rules.body: Purpose is the ONLY criterion scored 0–3. All others are scored 0–7.

rules.title: No single criterion weighting decides pass/fail
rules.body: OET does not publish a simple pass/fail weighting formula that makes two criteria universally decisive.

rules.title: Genre and Style significant
rules.body: Genre and Style has significant impact on the overall result.

rules.title: Language does not need to be perfect
rules.body: Language does not need to be perfect. Most OET failures result from poor content selection, not grammar errors.

rules.title: No universal regulator pass threshold
rules.body: Do not convert descriptors into a universal regulator pass threshold; regulator requirements vary.

rules.title: Real-clinic test
rules.body: Could this be sent clinically is a useful heuristic, not the official pass/fail formula.

rules.title: Assessment is holistic
rules.body: Assessment is holistic. Do not attempt to calculate an exact score.

rules.title: One blank line after the Re: line
rules.body: Salutation and Re: line remain consecutive. After the Re: line there MUST be one blank line before the introduction. Preserve this spacing in stored text, rendering, exports and candidate view.
exemplarPhrases:
Dear Dr Still,
Re: Mr David Taylor, aged 55

I am writing to ...

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard; flag a missing blank line after the Re: line under Organisation & Layout. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.
sourceRefs: Rev8 §2 Blank line after Re: line

rules.title: Salutation and Re: line consecutive
rules.body: No blank line between the salutation and the Re: line; they are the only two consecutive lines with no blank line between them.
exemplarPhrases:
Dear Dr Smith,
Re: Ms Garcia, DOB: 1 January 1995

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: One date-format family and four-digit years
rules.body: Use one date-format family throughout each letter (written, slash or dot — never mixed) and always a four-digit year.
exemplarPhrases: 13 June 2020 ... on 29 June 2014

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard; any single date-format family is accepted when it is used consistently with four-digit years. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: DOB written as "DOB:" + date
rules.body: Write the date of birth as "DOB:" followed by the date in the letter's date family; never "D.O.B", "DOB 01.01.1995" or "DOB not provided".
exemplarPhrases: Re: Mrs Melanie Wright, DOB: 8 June 1973

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: No brackets or placeholders
rules.body: The final letter contains no round, square or curly brackets and no placeholder text such as [Name] or {Surname}.
exemplarPhrases: dalteparin, also known as Fragmin,

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Descriptive numbers as words
rules.body: Write descriptive/general numbers as words. Use digits only for age, dates, vital signs, investigation/lab values, medication doses and clinical measurements.
exemplarPhrases: every six hours for four days

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: detected as a Major language point; the clinical-number exceptions (age, dates, vital signs, investigation/lab values, medication doses, clinical measurements) are never flagged. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: No emotional or editorial wording
rules.body: Do not use emotional/editorial words such as suffering/suffered, unfortunately, fortunately, regrettably or sadly. Keep wording factual and neutral.
exemplarPhrases: He had attacks on 1 June 2010 and 1 September 2010.

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard; any suffer/suffered/suffering, unfortunately, fortunately, regrettably or sadly blocks publication. CANDIDATE: unfortunately/fortunately/regrettably/sadly are always flagged; suffered/suffering is flagged only when used as emotional editorialising, never as the standard factual clinical verb for a diagnosed event. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: No judgmental disease or behaviour labels
rules.body: Do not label a person by a disease/behaviour (asthmatic, hypertensive, smoker, drinker, non-compliant, anxious). Use factual forms: has asthma, has hypertension, smokes ..., reported difficulty adhering ....
exemplarPhrases: Mr Weir smokes twenty cigarettes a day.

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard; the factual forms (has asthma, smokes ..., reported difficulty adhering to ...) are accepted in any professional wording. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Never "the patient" as the person reference
rules.body: Do not use "the patient" (or "a patient at this practice") as a substitute for the person in the final letter prose. Use the name form or a pronoun.
exemplarPhrases: Mr Weir smokes ...

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard; the name form or a pronoun is required as the person reference. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Name at the first mention of every body paragraph
rules.body: Adults: first mention in each body paragraph = title + surname; children: first name; later mentions in the same paragraph use he/she/him/her/his.
exemplarPhrases: Mr Weir first presented on 29 June 2014 ...

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard in every paragraph after the introduction, closure included. CANDIDATE: hard in the body paragraphs between the introduction and the closure; pronouns are correct for later mentions in the same paragraph. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.
sourceRefs: Rev8 §2 Patient naming rule - exact operational form

rules.title: Do not repeat the full name after the Re: line
rules.body: Do not repeat the full first + last name in the letter after it has been used in the Re: line (the introduction included).
exemplarPhrases: I am writing to refer Mr Taylor ...

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: No relationship label for a named patient
rules.body: When the patient is named, do not use "your mother", "your father" or another relationship label as the normal patient reference; use the approved name form at the first mention in each body paragraph, then pronouns.
exemplarPhrases: Mrs Ramsey will continue ranitidine, 150 mg twice daily ...

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard; a letter addressed to a relative still uses the approved name form (e.g. Mrs Ramsey). Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.
sourceRefs: Rev7 §13 Patient naming in family-recipient letters

rules.title: Model Answer opens with "I am writing to ..."
rules.body: Every generated Model Answer introduction begins with "I am writing to ..." followed by the task purpose (refer, request, update, inform, transfer, outline). Candidate answers may use a different professional opening if the purpose is immediately clear; no template matching.
exemplarPhrases: I am writing to outline the medication regime for Mrs Ramsey ...

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard; the introduction must begin with "I am writing to ..." followed by the task purpose. CANDIDATE: never required (Acceptable Alternative); any professional opening whose purpose is immediately clear is accepted and no template matching is applied. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Universal contact-offer closure
rules.body: Every Model Answer closure, in every profession and letter type, ends with a professional offer to contact the writer, e.g. "Should there be any queries, kindly do not hesitate to contact me." Semantic equivalents are acceptable; candidate grading judges meaning, not exact wording.
exemplarPhrases: Should there be any queries, kindly do not hesitate to contact me.

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard; the contact offer is the final sentence of the closure. CANDIDATE: the meaning is required anywhere in the closure, in any professional wording; semantic equivalents are accepted and exact wording is never required. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Urgent closure: "at your earliest convenience" then contact offer
rules.body: An urgent-referral Model Answer closure includes the urgent action with the canonical phrase "at your earliest convenience" and then finishes with the universal contact-offer sentence. A candidate may use any clear professional urgent wording, including "urgent"/"urgently"; never penalised for not copying the Model Answer.
exemplarPhrases: I would be grateful if you could assess Mr Taylor at your earliest convenience. Should there be any queries, kindly do not hesitate to contact me.

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard; the closure request contains "at your earliest convenience" and is followed by the universal contact-offer sentence. CANDIDATE: Acceptable Alternative; any clear professional urgent closure wording, including "urgent"/"urgently", is accepted and a candidate is never penalised for not copying the Model Answer. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: "Urgent" only in the introduction (Model Answer)
rules.body: In an urgent-referral Model Answer use "urgent/urgently" in the introduction only; the closure implies urgency with "at your earliest convenience". Candidates are never penalised for repeating urgency.
exemplarPhrases: I am writing to urgently refer ...

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard; "urgent"/"urgently" appears in the introduction only. CANDIDATE: never penalised for repeating urgency. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Urgent referral: today/current presentation first, even if brief
rules.body: Body paragraph 1 of an urgent referral is today's/the current acute presentation ONLY, kept as its own paragraph even when today's visit contains very little information; the next paragraph returns to the relevant earlier history in chronological order.
exemplarPhrases: On today's visit, Mr Taylor presented with ...

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard; body paragraph 1 is the current presentation only, kept as its own paragraph even if brief. CANDIDATE: hard; today's/current presentation first, then the relevant earlier history in chronological order. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.
sourceRefs: Rev8 §5 Latest owner override: minimal information in today's visit

rules.title: Urgent purpose explicit in the introduction
rules.body: An urgent referral introduction makes the urgent purpose explicit. Candidate grading assesses whether the purpose and urgency are clear, not exact template wording.
exemplarPhrases: I am writing to urgently refer Mr Taylor for rheumatological assessment of ...

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: the purpose and the urgency must be clear; exact template wording is not required. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Hospital urgent referral: active conditions with current medication
rules.body: In a hospital urgent referral mention every ongoing medical condition for which the person takes active medication, with the relevant current medication and dose (only from the case notes).
exemplarPhrases: Mr Taylor has hypertension, for which he takes ramipril, 5 mg daily.

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard, checked by the independent semantic Model Answer validator (no deterministic detector). CANDIDATE: AI-graded under Content, counting only conditions and medicines present in the case notes. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Closure does not duplicate the introduction's request
rules.body: The introduction states the purpose/request clearly; the closure must not repeat the same request wording verbatim. It may restate the needed action concisely where functionally necessary. The final contact-offer sentence does not count as duplicate-request wording.
exemplarPhrases: Intro: '... for rheumatological assessment of an acute gout flare.' Closure: 'I would be grateful if you could assess Mr Taylor at your earliest convenience.'

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard for verbatim repetition only; a concise restatement of the needed action and the final contact-offer sentence are not duplication. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Linker vocabulary
rules.body: Generated Model Answers avoid but, so, hence, furthermore, moreover and also as routine linking devices. Prefer however, therefore, thus, consequently, subsequently, in addition, in addition to this/that, or additionally only when logically appropriate; direct sentences are preferable to unnecessary linkers (normally no more than 1-2 per paragraph).
exemplarPhrases: In addition, his brother has gout.

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard; any occurrence of but, so, hence, furthermore, moreover or also blocks publication. CANDIDATE: hence/furthermore/moreover and clause-joining but/so are detected as vocabulary-preference feedback, not grammar errors; also is advisory only. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Linker punctuation
rules.body: At the beginning of a sentence capitalise the linker and place a comma after it (However, / Therefore, / Consequently, / Subsequently, / In addition, / Additionally,). When the linker joins two complete independent clauses use a semicolon before it, lowercase it and place a comma after it (...; however, ...). Do not apply the pattern mechanically when the grammar does not contain two complete clauses.
exemplarPhrases: Her pain settled; however, she reported new swelling.

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard for genuine run-ons and comma splices only; adverbial use (e.g. "was therefore referred") is never flagged. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Medication-list syntax
rules.body: Single item: Drug, dose. Two items: Drug, dose and Drug, dose. Three or more: Drug, dose; Drug, dose; and Drug, dose. Keep a comma between medicine and dose, semicolons between items and "and" before the final item; translate Latin frequency abbreviations; capitalise trade names, generic names lowercase; never invent a dose absent from the case notes.
exemplarPhrases: ranitidine, 150 mg twice daily; atorvastatin, 20 mg each morning; and dalteparin, 2500 IU by injection

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Space between value and unit
rules.body: Keep a space between a numeric dose/clinical value and its unit where standard (500 mg, 2 g, 1.8 g, 6.37 mmol/L).
exemplarPhrases: 6.37 mmol/L; 2 g; 10 mg

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Age not duplicated between Re: line and introduction
rules.body: If the age is already in the Re: line, do not repeat the same age in the introduction unless a specific approved exception applies.
exemplarPhrases: Re: Mr David Taylor, aged 55 / I am writing to refer Mr Taylor for ...

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Sign-off: professional designation only
rules.body: Yours sincerely when the recipient is named, Yours faithfully when genuinely unnamed. After the closing phrase use the professional designation only (Doctor, Nurse, Pharmacist, Physiotherapist ...) unless the task supplies the exact writer name; never hospital, department, address, phone or email beneath it. Leave the approved one (at most two) blank line(s) between the closing phrase and the designation.
exemplarPhrases:
Yours sincerely,

Pharmacist

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard; a missing designation is advisory only. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Body 180-200 words (body only)
rules.body: Body word-count guide remains 180-200 words, BODY ONLY (introduction to closure). Mandatory for generated Model Answers; advisory feedback for candidates.

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard; 180-200 words counted from the introduction to the closure. CANDIDATE: advisory feedback only. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: At least two body paragraphs
rules.body: Use at least two body paragraphs, typically two to three; avoid one-paragraph letters and unnecessary fragmentation.

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: No today's exact date and no "yesterday" in the body
rules.body: Do not write today's exact date in the body (use "On today's visit"/"On today's presentation"); avoid "yesterday" (use "one day prior"/"one day ago").
exemplarPhrases: On today's visit, Mr Taylor presented with ...

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: No contractions
rules.body: No contractions in formal OET letter output.
exemplarPhrases: does not

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: advisory (Genre & Style note). Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Routine referral order and background placement
rules.body: Start with the main complaint/current reason for referral and organise subsequent paragraphs deliberately rather than copying case notes mechanically. Place relevant medical, family, social and special-habit background near the end, before the closure, when relevant and permitted by the letter type. Do not include irrelevant background merely to fill a category.

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard, checked by the independent semantic Model Answer validator. CANDIDATE: AI-graded organisation; different valid organisation is accepted. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Discharge/update letter-type exceptions
rules.body: The background-placement rule does not force medical/family/social/special-habit history into every letter: discharge/update letters may exclude family history, social history, smoking/drinking, previous medical history or occupation because the recipient already knows the patient.

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard, checked by the independent semantic Model Answer validator. CANDIDATE: AI-graded relevance. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Professional clinical register
rules.body: Use supported clinical wording rather than weak, colloquial or redundant phrasing (fatigue not tired/sluggish; MRI not MRI imaging; felt a popping sensation not felt something pop; does not currently have a GP not with no GP).
exemplarPhrases: reported fatigue

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: advisory. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: The closure remains a closure
rules.body: Management and history belong before the closure; after the closing request do not return to management advice (e.g. "She was advised ...").
exemplarPhrases: Mrs Wright was advised to avoid weight-bearing ... (body). I would be grateful if you could arrange ... (closure).

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard (every violation blocks publication). CANDIDATE: hard. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Introduction tense
rules.body: Present simple and present perfect remain acceptable introduction tenses; present continuous is also acceptable when it correctly describes a current presentation ("who is presenting with features suggestive of ..."). The introduction stays concise and patient-specific with the purpose immediately clear.
exemplarPhrases: I am writing to refer Mr Weir, who is presenting with features suggestive of multiple sclerosis, ...

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard, checked by the independent semantic Model Answer validator. CANDIDATE: never penalised for present simple, present perfect or (when it correctly describes a current presentation) present continuous. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Paragraph spacing survives storage and rendering
rules.body: Address block, one blank line, date, one blank line, salutation + Re: line, one blank line, introduction, one blank line between every body paragraph, one blank line before the closure and before the closing phrase, approved spacing before the designation. The spacing must survive storage, API transport, HTML rendering and the candidate-facing Model Answer component; a rule-engine PASS with broken visual spacing is a FAIL.

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard; a rule-engine PASS with broken visual spacing is a FAIL. CANDIDATE: the layout rules as listed. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Factual fidelity and certainty level
rules.body: Use only facts present in the exact case notes and task; never invent a diagnosis, test, treatment, dose, route, frequency, date or request, and preserve the certainty level (a prophylactic intention is never upgraded to a guarantee such as "will prevent blood clots").
exemplarPhrases: dalteparin, 2500 IU by injection to reduce the risk of blood clots

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: hard, enforced by grounding and the independent semantic Model Answer validator. CANDIDATE: AI-graded under Content. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

rules.title: Candidate grading: zero Model Answer similarity
rules.body: The candidate grader applies the same source-of-truth rules but never uses Model Answer similarity, phrase matching or template matching; genuinely correct alternative wording, synonyms, professional phrasing and different valid organisation are not penalised. Model Answer similarity contribution to the score is ZERO.

params.aiGradingLogic: MODEL ANSWER: not applicable. CANDIDATE: policy; the candidate grader applies the same source-of-truth rules but never uses Model Answer similarity, phrase matching or template matching, and genuinely correct alternative wording, synonyms, professional phrasing and different valid organisation are not penalised. Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO to the candidate score.

adult.reLine: Title + full name (e.g. Re: Ms Sara Miller D.O.B: 01/01/1984)
adult.bodyFirstMention: Title + last name (e.g. Ms Miller presented with...)

child.reLine: Full name only, NO title (e.g. Re: Sara Miller D.O.B: 01/01/2015)
child.bodyFirstMention: First name only (e.g. Sara presented with...)

ageOnly.reLine: Re: Ms Sara Miller, aged 40 (lowercase 'aged', no colon, no 'Age:' prefix)

letterSkeleton: Body paragraphs (one blank line between each, 2–4 total)
